title: Prayer in Public Schools
short: Engel v. Vitale (1962) struck down a state-composed prayer; Abington v. Schempp (1963) struck down school-sponsored Bible reading; Lee v. Weisman (1992) and Santa Fe v. Doe (2000) struck down prayers at graduation and football games; private prayer by students is protected.
trouble: Students think students may not pray at public school. The cases bar school-sponsored prayer; private prayer by students is protected.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Public schools are where the Establishment tests were tested most. Students are young, attendance is required, and schools carry the state's authority, so the Court has paid special attention to pressure on students. This unit teaches the religion clauses as law: what the clauses say, the tests courts use and the holdings. It takes no position on any faith or on religion itself.

head: Case
Practice
Result
rows: a short prayer written by New York's Board of Regents, said aloud each morning; students could be excused
struck down: government may not compose official prayers, even voluntary and nondenominational ones
school-sponsored Bible reading and recitation of the Lord's Prayer at the start of the day
struck down; the Court added that teaching about religion, its history and literature, is permitted
a moment of silence law amended to add "or voluntary prayer"
struck down: its purpose was to endorse prayer (plain moments of silence were not at issue)
a principal invited a rabbi to give prayers at a middle school graduation
struck down: subtle coercion to stand or remain silent
Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe (2000)
a student, chosen under a school policy, gave a prayer over the loudspeaker before football games

blocks.html: The line runs between government prayer and private prayer. Students may pray alone or together, read religious books in free time, and form religious clubs on the same terms as other clubs (the Equal Access Act of 1984, upheld in Board of Education v. Mergens, 1990). Teachers may teach about religion. What schools may not do is lead, compose or sponsor prayer. In each case above, the Court asked who was really speaking: the school, through its officials, policies or loudspeaker, or a private person.
Schools may not sponsor prayer: Engel (official prayer), Abington (Bible reading), Lee (graduation), Santa Fe (football games). Private religious expression by students is protected.

blocks.title: A student's speech
blocks.q: A valedictorian, choosing her own words in a speech the school does not review for content, thanks God. Is the school violating the Establishment Clause?
steps: The question is whether the speech is the school's or the student's.
If the student chooses her own words without school direction, it is her private expression.
Courts look closely at how much the school controls the speech; in Santa Fe, the school's policy and loudspeaker made the prayer school-sponsored.
blocks.a: Likely no: private student expression is protected.

blocks.title: Voluntary prayer
blocks.q: A school district writes a short nondenominational prayer and lets students leave the room if they wish. Does voluntariness save it?
steps: Engel v. Vitale (1962) faced exactly this: an official, nondenominational prayer with an excusal option.
The Court held that government may not compose official prayers at all.
blocks.a: No; Engel struck down such a prayer.

blocks.html: Thinking students may not pray at public school. The cases bar school-sponsored prayer. Private prayer by students is protected, and religious student groups may meet on the same terms as other groups.
